title: The Famous Lucena
reviewNotes: Three branches, 20 exact positions beginning in stable five-piece Lucena diagram after ...Rc1 at 85 seconds. Fourth-rank preparation, king separation and king zigzag reach Rc4 bridge. Independent rook trade allows promotion; independent Kb5 instead of interposition loses the pawn and draws. Earlier six-piece game sequence remains context.
transcript: After 14,000 games online, I finally did it. I got one of the coolest textbook end game positions in a real over-the-board rated game, and I want to teach you how you can win this position, too. Here's the position. I'm playing white, and I have two pawns as an advantage, and I am clearly pushing for a win. But how? I cannot just keep moving my king. The rook is always going to check me. So, I have to find shelter somewhere, and I decide that I am going to find shelter in front of my own rook. Leaving this pawn here to perish. And if you don't know the position that I'm about to show you, this might seem like nonsense. Why would we give up one of the two pawns that we are trying to use to win? But the thing is, I had seen from afar that in just a couple of moves, we would have ended up in a position that looked something like this. This is called the Lucena position, and every chess player worth their money should know how to convert this. Here's the ingredients. We have a pawn one step away from promoting, but our own king is in front of the pawn, and there is one rook left for each player. Now, here's what's interesting about this position. Black can always keep an eye on this pawn, and as soon as we try to move the king away from the pawn, for example, like this, black is going to start giving us checks, and no matter where we go with the king, there's always going to be a check with the rook, making it impossible to promote the pawn. But of course, if we stay in front of the pawn, we cannot make space for it. So, to win this, there is a four-step procedure that we need to follow. The first step is to bring our own rook to the fourth rank, like this. Now, black is either going to move the rook or the king. The second step is to make sure that this king is a little bit further away from the action, and so we're going to give him a check with the rook. Notice that if the king comes here, now we can use it as a shield against his own rook. The rook cannot take this pawn, because after this check, we are forcing the king away from the defense of the rook. If it persists, we're going to give another check, and then win like this. So, naturally, the king will walk away like this. Step three is going to bring our king two steps away from the pawn. And here's how we do that. We move the king, the rook is going to try and check us because otherwise we promote. We bring the king in front, and after this other check, of course, we cannot come here right away. So, we have to put in a zigzag move like this, and after the other check, now we can come to c5. And finally, the last step. After this rook check, we are finally ready to win this position. And that is why we placed the rook on the fourth rank. We can play rook to c4. The black rook has no way to come and stop the pawn, and if it ever trades the rook, of course, we're going to win. The king is too far away to stop the pawn. And so, in this position, my opponent resigned. And now you know how you can win the Lucena position.
